newsitem.title: UK: U.S. derivatives investors view EMU with caution.
newsitem.headline: U.S. derivatives investors view EMU with caution.

text.p: Uncertainties surrounding the implementation of European economic and monetary union (EMU) are scaring off U.S. investors, an industry conference heard on Wednesday.

Speaking at the International Derivatives Conference in London, Todd Petzel, chief investment officer of the Common Fund said it was proving difficult for end-users to accept the confusion over how the new euro landscape will look.
"The end-users in the trenches are worried that you don't even know the value of your portfolio, when you don't know what currencies will be in the euro," he said.
"The reaction of many managers is just to back away," he said.

Recent upsets along the road to EMU, notably the shock left-wing victory in the French election and the row over Germany's plans to revalue its gold and currency assets, have also heightened U.S. concerns.

U.S.-based Galen Burghardt, senior vice president of Dean Witter Institutional Futures, said the rise in the spread between implied volatility of options on the three-month PIBOR interest rate futures and on the comparable euromark contracts suggested there were significant worries.
"The move out in the implied volatility spread is not a sign of a confident market," he said. "I'm not the only one who's sceptical."

TJ Lim, global head of fixed income and currency derivatives at UBS Ltd, said he expected fierce competition between exchanges to result in more trade within the euro bloc, but issues such as ability to deliver would probably create problems.
"With many issuers, and many benchmarks, deciding what is the cheapest-to-deliver will become very important," Lim said.
Investment in emerging market currencies and products could also become more active, he said.
Lim said while currency risk would clearly decline, credit risk would gain in importance, as debt issuers would have to target their issuance at a broader market.
"Issuers who have been used to focusing on a home market will have to look at pan-European issues," he said.
"On the European side, not knowing what the euro will look like is holding people back," he said.
